content: The survey was designed to assess the feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and appropriateness of various strategies for improving hepatitis C (HCV) care and treatment. Participants were adults aged 18 years or older who were either living with or affected by HCV and had confirmed their willingness to participate. The survey explored four key questions: 1. Decentralization: Can HCV care and treatment be effectively and safely delivered in lower-level health facilities? 2. Integration: Can HCV care and treatment be effectively and safely integrated with other health services? 3. Task-shifting: Can HCV testing, care, and treatment be effectively and safely delivered by non-specialists? 4. Point-of-care viral load testing: Can point-of-care HCV viral load testing serve as an alternative to laboratory-based assays to improve uptake of testing and treatment? The survey was developed with input from Coalition PLUS and the World Hepatitis Alliance, incorporating community knowledge and experiences regarding challenges in accessing HCV care. It consisted of 42 multiple-choice questions, some with free-text options for additional comments. The survey was divided into two sections: (1) participants’ experiences with HCV testing and treatment, and (2) their preferences for simplifying HCV services, including testing locations, same-day testing and treatment, integration, and task-shifting. The survey was estimated to take 15 minutes to complete and was only available in English due to time constraints. It was created using SurveyMonkey and promoted through social media, mailing lists, and direct contacts by Coalition PLUS, the World Hepatitis Alliance, regional WHO offices, and the Treatment Action Group. Data Collection and Analysis The survey was launched on September 8, 2021, and data collection lasted two weeks, closing on September 22, 2021. A total of 210 participants from 49 countries completed the survey. Most respondents (71%) were aged 26–55 years, and the majority were male (56%), followed by females (40%), transgender individuals (1%), and gender non-binary individuals (2%). The largest proportion of participants resided in Nigeria (23%), followed by the United States (20%), Australia, and the United Kingdom (7% each). Most participants lived in middle-income (52%) or high-income (40%) countries, with 8% residing in low-income countries. Urban or large city areas were the most common places of residence (68%), and 83% of participants had completed tertiary education. Key Findings Testing Preferences: Among participants who had been tested for HCV, hospitals were the most common testing sites (24%), followed by primary care clinics (20%), laboratories (15%), and community-based organizations (13%). However, when asked about their preferred testing locations, 44% chose community-based organizations, 35% preferred self-testing, and 28% selected hospitals or primary care clinics. This indicates a strong preference for decentralized and community-based testing options. Treatment Preferences: Most participants who had received HCV treatment were treated at hospitals (64%) or primary care clinics (22%). When asked about their preferred treatment locations, 50% chose community-based organizations, 39% preferred hospitals, and 29% selected general practitioners. A significant proportion (54%) expressed a preference for receiving treatment at the same site as testing, highlighting the importance of service integration. Convenience and Accessibility: The majority of participants (91%) preferred to be tested and treated at the same location, citing convenience (34%) and continuity of care (33%) as the main reasons. Participants emphasized the importance of having HCV services integrated with other health services and delivered by non-specialists to improve accessibility. Non-judgmental Care: For marginalized populations, such as people who inject drugs and those living with HIV, the most important consideration for testing and treatment locations was a non-judgmental and non-stigmatizing environment. This was prioritized over proximity to home or cost. Task-shifting and Decentralization: While the expertise of trained medical professionals was valued, participants also expressed strong support for services provided by trained peer and community workers. This highlights the need for culturally competent and community-friendly care. Specialist Care: Despite a preference for decentralized services, participants still valued the role of specialist doctors for discussing health needs related to HCV. However, trained community or peer workers were also highly regarded, particularly among people who inject drugs. Limitations The survey had several limitations: The sampling method and small sample size limit the generalizability of the findings. Online surveys may not reach populations without regular internet access, such as homeless individuals or those experiencing marginalization. The survey was only available in English, which may have excluded non-English-speaking participants. Most respondents lived in urban areas, potentially underrepresenting the challenges faced by those in rural settings. The survey was not extensively piloted, and a fully participatory approach involving affected populations in its development could have strengthened the results. Recommendations Expanding testing opportunities in diverse settings, including self-testing, is essential to increase HCV testing uptake. Decentralized services are particularly beneficial for people who inject drugs and other marginalized groups. Integrating testing and treatment services in the same location can improve linkage to care and treatment adherence. Task-shifting to trained peer and community workers should be considered to enhance accessibility and cultural competence. Efforts should focus on providing a range of HCV testing and treatment options to meet the diverse needs of different populations and settings. Additional research is needed to understand the preferences and barriers faced by marginalized populations not reached by traditional health systems. In conclusion, the findings underscore the importance of decentralizing and integrating HCV services, offering culturally competent care, and expanding task-shifting to improve access and outcomes for diverse populations.
